summary: Yemen lies at the southwestern tip of the Arabian Peninsula, the site of the ancient Kingdom of Sheba and the frankincense trade, and in recent years has suffered greatly from civil war and a humanitarian crisis.

ranking.name: Islam (Sunni)
ranking.description: Islam reached Yemen in the 7th century during the lifetime of the Prophet Muhammad, when the Persian governor then ruling the region converted and the Yemeni tribes also embraced it one after another. The south, the western coastal plain and eastern Hadramawt follow the Shafi'i school of Sunni Islam, and families of Sufi scholars from Hadramawt spread Islam to Southeast Asia and East Africa through maritime trade. The two periods of Ottoman rule in Yemen and British rule in Aden also strengthened the position of Sunnism in the south, making it the majority of the population.

ranking.name: Islam (Shia, Zaydi)
ranking.description: In 897 the imam al-Hadi Yahya established a Zaydi imamate in Sa'dah in the north, and thereafter Zaydi imams intermittently ruled the northern highlands for more than a thousand years, until the 1962 revolution overthrew the dynasty and established a republic. In the 1990s the Houthi movement, stressing a Zaydi revival, arose in the north, and in 2014 it seized the capital, Sana'a, triggering a civil war that remains unresolved. Zaydi followers are concentrated in the northern highlands and make up about 40 percent of the country.

ranking.name: Others
ranking.description: The history of the Jews of Yemen goes back to ancient times, and in the 6th century Dhu Nuwas, king of the Himyarite Kingdom, even converted to Judaism. In 1949-1950 Israel airlifted about fifty thousand Yemeni Jews to Israel in "Operation Magic Carpet," and only a tiny number remain in the country. Others include foreign Christians, Isma'ilis in the Haraz Mountains of the north, and long-persecuted followers of the Bahá'í Faith.

religion.background: The ancient Yemeni kingdoms such as Sheba and Himyar followed polytheism, and Judaism and Christianity also appeared later. Islam arrived in the 7th century; the northern highlands were ruled by Zaydi imams from the 9th century, while the south and the coast were mainly Sunni of the Shafi'i school. The 1962 revolution in the north ended imamic rule, the south became independent from Britain in 1967, and north and south were unified in 1990. After the Zaydi-based Houthi movement seized Sana'a in 2014, religious and sectarian antagonism became an important background to the civil war.

ranking.name: Sanaani Arabic
ranking.description: Sanaani Arabic is the dialect of the northern highlands and the area around the capital, Sana'a, and preserves many features of Classical Arabic. After Islam arrived, Arabic gradually replaced the ancient South Arabian languages such as Sabaic; the northern highlands are densely populated, and Sana'a has long been the capital of the Zaydi imams and then of the republic, so this dialect has the largest number of speakers in the country.

ranking.name: Ta'izzi-Adeni Arabic
ranking.description: Ta'izzi-Adeni Arabic is spoken in the central and southern regions, including Ta'izz, Ibb and the port city of Aden. Britain ruled Aden from 1839 to 1967, leading the local dialect to absorb many English and Hindi loanwords; the Ta'izz area is densely populated and has a higher level of education, so this dialect has many speakers and great influence in the south.

ranking.name: Hadrami Arabic
ranking.description: Hadrami Arabic is spoken in the Hadramawt region in the east, where the population is smaller. In the 18th-20th centuries large numbers of Hadramis migrated to Indonesia, Singapore, Malaysia and East Africa to do business, and returning migrants brought back Malay and other vocabulary to their homeland, giving this dialect a distinctive overseas flavor.

language.history: Ancient Yemen used Old South Arabian languages such as Sabaic and Himyaritic, written in the distinctive "Musnad" script carved on stone steles. After Islamization in the 7th century, Arabic gradually replaced these languages and became the common language of the country. Today the east of Yemen and Socotra Island still preserve "Modern South Arabian" languages such as Mehri and Socotri, which are not Arabic dialects but independent languages. Since the north-south unification of 1990, Standard Arabic has been the sole official language, and differences among regional dialects remain obvious.

ranking.name: Saltah
ranking.description: A mutton-stock-based stew with minced meat, potatoes, tomatoes and spices is brought to the table boiling in a scorching stone pot, topped with a layer of fenugreek sauce whipped into foam.
ranking.history: Saltah is regarded as the national dish of Yemen and is especially popular in the northern capital, Sana'a, traditionally the star of lunch, eaten by tearing fresh flatbread and dipping it in. Fenugreek is a spice that has been grown on the Arabian Peninsula since ancient times, and when whipped into a green foam it has a distinctive bitter fragrance. Yemeni men often gather after a hearty lunch to chew qat, so saltah is closely tied to Yemen's distinctive social life.

ranking.name: Mandi
ranking.description: Meat of lamb or chicken marinated in spices is hung in an underground clay oven with spiced rice placed below, then sealed and cooked for several hours, the juices dripping into the rice, leaving the meat tender.
ranking.history: Mandi originated in the Hadramawt region in the east, and its name is believed to be related to the Arabic word for "dew," describing the moist, juicy meat. Baking in a pit dug in the ground suits deserts and dry regions and also allows food to be prepared for large numbers of guests at once. In the 18th-20th centuries large numbers of Hadramis migrated to the Gulf, Southeast Asia and East Africa, bringing mandi to Gulf countries such as Saudi Arabia and making it one of the most popular rice dishes on the Arabian Peninsula.

ranking.name: Honey mille-feuille bread (Bint al-Sahn)
ranking.description: Many layers of thin dough are brushed with ghee, stacked and baked, then drizzled with Yemeni honey and sprinkled with nigella seeds when it comes out of the oven; crisp outside, soft inside, sweet and rich.
ranking.history: The name of this dessert means "daughter of the plate," and it is an important dessert for entertaining guests and at weddings and festivals in Yemen. Yemen has been known for honey since ancient times, and the sidr honey of Hadramawt and Wadi Do'an is regarded as among the most precious honey in the world; bint al-sahn is the dish that shows off this specialty. Traditionally it is served hot as a dessert after a hearty lunch, along with a cup of spiced coffee or tea.

ranking.name: Fahsa
ranking.description: Stewed lamb is shredded finely and brought to a bubbling boil with stock in a stone pot, topped with fenugreek foam, and scooped up with bread to eat.
ranking.history: Fahsa is a traditional lunch of the Sana'a area, similar to saltah but centered on plenty of stewed lamb and regarded as a heartier version. The stone pots used by Yemenis are carved from local soapstone and keep heat for a long time, so the food is still boiling when served. This dish often appears at family gatherings, religious holidays and when entertaining guests, eaten with freshly baked Yemeni flatbread.

ranking.name: Zhug (zhoug) chili sauce
ranking.description: Fresh green chili peppers, cilantro, garlic, cumin and cardamom are pounded into a green chili sauce that is fiery and pungent, and can be served with bread, meat and soups.
ranking.history: This chili sauce is traditionally pounded by hand in a stone mortar and is a basic condiment on the table of every Yemeni household. Chili peppers originated in the Americas and came to the Arabian Peninsula after the 16th century via the Ottoman Empire and Indian Ocean trade, quickly becoming an important ingredient in Yemeni food. In 1949-1950, when Yemeni Jews emigrated in large numbers to Israel, they brought this sauce there, and under the name "zhug" it became one of Israel's most common hot sauces.
